metadata.title: The Best House On The Block Costs The Most: RDDT

content.text:
Reddit is delivering leading growth but commands a top-of-the-market price, forcing investors to decide if its operational lead is already paid for.
Reddit (RDDT), the sprawling collection of online communities, has seen its stock climb +21% over the last three months, trading around $178.04 a share. The platform thrives on what its CEO calls "authentic human conversation," a resource it sells to advertisers looking for high-intent audiences. Among its social media peers, however, Reddit presents a sharp mismatch: it is both the group's fastest operator and its most expensive ticket. The question for investors is whether the market has this rank-ordering right, and if there is any upside left for a buyer at this price.
Reddit's growth is in a class of its own.
By the numbers, Reddit's performance laps its competitors. The company's revenue grew 71% over the last twelve months, a figure that dwarfs the 28% growth at Meta Platforms and 20% at Alphabet. This isn't a one-off surge; management recently highlighted its "eighth consecutive quarter of over 60% revenue growth." This momentum is fueled by a booming advertising business, where revenue grew 64% in the last quarter, driven by a more than 70% year-over-year increase in active advertisers. The company is successfully rolling out new tools, like its Reddit Max ad platform, to attract more spending.
This earns it a premium valuation. Reddit trades at 48.2 times earnings, far richer than Meta's 20.1. The market is clearly paying up for the growth story, betting that Reddit's unique position as a hub for human-led discussion will become more valuable as the rest of the web fills with automated content.
But a user-growth shadow fuels the debate
While the company's monetization engine is firing, its user growth is facing turbulence. On its latest earnings call, management acknowledged that growth in daily active users from its own product improvements was "offset by a decline in search referrals." This reliance on traffic from external search engines, where the company has "low" visibility, is the core of the bear case. Investors worry that as search evolves, this critical source of new users could diminish, stalling the growth that underpins the stock's premium.
Management insists it is not building for "drive-by traffic" and is focused on converting its large base of weekly visitors into daily, direct users. It points to early progress, with new app user retention up 50% year-over-year on a relative basis. Still, the market remains skeptical.
